---
title: "Getting started"
description: "Branch model, caller files, secrets and the GitHub App."
---

## Branch model

The workflows assume a two-branch model:

- **`dev`** — integration branch. Feature branches are merged here via pull
  requests, which run the [checks](r-cmd-check.qmd) and the
  [bot suggestions](suggestions.qmd).
- **`main`** — release branch. Only `dev` is merged into `main`; that merge
  is automated and triggers the [release](release.qmd).

Most example callers use `branches: [dev]` or `branches: [main]` in their
triggers. If your branches are named differently, adjust those triggers and
the `allowed-head` / `sweep-base` inputs.

Your package needs no other preparation. For example, the
[test suggestions](test-suggest.qmd) set up `testthat` themselves if the
package doesn't use it yet.

## Caller files

Every workflow page has an example caller to copy into
`.github/workflows/` of your repository. A few rules apply to all of them:

- **Reference `@main`.** Changes here reach your repository on its next run —
  there is nothing to update on your side.
- **Grant permissions on the calling job.** A reusable workflow can't have
  more permissions than its caller grants. Each page lists what its workflow
  needs under *Permissions*; the examples already include it.
- **Pass secrets explicitly.** Each workflow declares the secrets it reads.
  Map them one by one, as the examples do, rather than
  `secrets: inherit` — two workflows may need different values under the
  same name (see [Claude setup](claude-setup.qmd)).

## Secrets

The names on the left are what the examples use; you can choose your own,
as long as the caller maps them to the workflow's secret names.

| Repository secret | Used by | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `APP_CLIENT_ID`, `APP_PRIVATE_KEY` | release, bot suggestions | GitHub App for bot pushes and PRs — see below |
| `CODECOV_TOKEN` | R CMD check | Coverage upload; required for private repositories |
| `ANTHROPIC_ORG_ID` | roxygen / test suggestions | Anthropic organization ID — can be an organization-level secret |
| `ANTHROPIC_SVAC_ID` | roxygen / test suggestions | Service account of this repository |
| `ANTHROPIC_FDRL_ROXYGEN`, `ANTHROPIC_FDRL_TESTS` | roxygen / test suggestions | Federation rule per workflow |

The three Anthropic IDs are set up in the Claude Console, see
[Claude setup](claude-setup.qmd).

## GitHub App {#github-app}

Several workflows push commits or open pull requests. Doing that with the
default `GITHUB_TOKEN` has two drawbacks:

- **Pull requests opened with `GITHUB_TOKEN` don't trigger workflows**, so
  required checks never run on a bot's suggestion PR and it can't be merged.
- **Rulesets can't exempt it**: the release has to push a version commit
  and tag to a protected `main`, which needs a *bypass actor*.

A GitHub App solves both. The workflows use it automatically when
`app-client-id` and `app-private-key` are passed, and fall back to a
`commit-push-pat` secret or `GITHUB_TOKEN` otherwise.

1. Create a GitHub App (in your organization's or your personal settings)
   with repository permissions **Contents** and **Pull requests** set to
   *Read and write* (**Metadata** *Read-only* is added automatically). No
   webhook is needed.
2. Generate a private key for it.
3. Install the App on the repositories that use these workflows.
4. Store the App's **Client ID** (on its settings page, starting with
   `Iv23li`, not the numeric App ID) and the private key as the secrets
   `APP_CLIENT_ID` and `APP_PRIVATE_KEY` — as organization secrets if
   several repositories share the App.
5. Add the App as a bypass actor in your `main` ruleset, see
   [Branch protection](branch-protection.qmd).

### Alternative: personal access token

Instead of the App, you can pass a personal access token as the
`commit-push-pat` secret (fine-grained: **Contents** and **Pull requests**
*Read and write* on the repository). Pull requests opened with it do
trigger workflows. The token order is App → PAT → `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

The App is still recommended: a PAT acts as its owner, so bot commits and
pull requests appear under their name, it stops working when they leave or
the token expires, and it can do everything its owner can.
